To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the physiological plasticity of extant fern species is greater than that of extant gymnosperm and angiosperm species, suggesting that the ferns were able to adapt more easily to the low [O2], high [CO2] atmosphere across the TJB, and thus may explain the ecological success of ferns following this mass extinction event.
the physiological plasticity of extant ferns and G. biloba species is markedly different following growth under an atmosphere similar to the TJB.

the photosynthetic responses of extant angiosperm, monilophyte and gymnosperm species to a simulated Triassic‐Jurassy atmosphere are species specific and that these responses may provide an insight into the underlying mechanisms of their ecological success and failure across the Triassic−Jurassic mass extinction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of atmospheric composition and the physiological plasticity of extant species, which may explain the contrasting ecological fates of Ginkgo and ferns during the TJB.
how the photosynthetic machinery of plants acclimates to a fluctuating [CO2]‐[O2] ratio and its potential impact on their evolutionary success.
the physiological plasticity of plants and the potential for this to influence plant evolution in the context of fluctuating atmospheric [O2]: [CO2].
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ferns were able to adapt their photosynthesis to low [O2], whereas Ginkgo could not.

the physiological plasticity of fern species was more robust than that of the angiosperm and Ginkgo species, and the latter species may have been more vulnerable to the low [O2] conditions that prevailed at the TJB.

the photosynthetic responses of the species tested here were not sufficient to explain the observed ecological patterns, but that the photosyntheses of the species are consistent with their ecological patterns.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the physiological plasticity of extant species is a useful tool for understanding the evolutionary history of plants.
the photosynthetic physiology of extant species is not necessarily a reliable proxy for the physiology of extinct species.
the ferns are more plastic than gymnosperms and angiosperms in terms of photosynthetic acclimation to a low [O2] environment, and the gymnosperms are more plastic than angiosperms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the [O2]: [CO2] ratio may have been a major driver of the ecological changes that occurred during the TJB.
the physiological responses of extant species to low [O2] and high [CO2] may provide valuable insights into the ecological fate of species across major extinction events.
the photosynthetic capacity of the C3 species studied is more plastic than that of the gymnosperm.
